span: The bar contained in Section 25 is limited by sub Section (1) of Section 18 of the MCOCA.
why: Court explains that MCOCA s.18 lifts the s.25 bar for confessions to senior police officers, but only subject to statutory safeguards; the general bar remains otherwise.

span: It is relevant and admissible against the maker of it.
why: Court's own conclusion that a confession recorded by a police officer under POTA s.32 is admissible against its maker (not against co-accused), an exception to ss.25-26.

span: such portion alone would be admissible under Section 27 of the Evidence Act, and not the entire confessional statements
why: Court holds confessions to police are barred by s.25 but the part leading to a discovery is admissible under s.27.

span: There cannot be any dispute that a confession made by the accused in police custody is an inadmissible confession.
why: Headnote: a confession in police custody is inadmissible, apart from the portion leading to recovery under s.27.

span: A confession made to a police officer under any circumstances is not admissible in evidence against the accused.
why: Court quotes Aghnoo Nagesia and then concludes ('Thus') that s.25 protection applies regardless of formal accusation, relying on the rule as imperative.

span: proof of the confession is prohibited by Section 25 of the Evidence Act
why: Court elaborates (applying Aghnoo Nagesia) that a confession to police is barred by s.25 except the portion within s.27.

span: has been referred to a larger Bench in the case of Tofan Singh v. State of Tamil Nadu
why: Notes that whether a s.67 NDPS statement is a confession is pending before a larger bench and proceeds on the premise of admissibility; no ruling on police confessions.
